content: To diagnose spinal injuries, plain X-rays of the spine remain a commonly utilized tool by most specialists and tertiary care centers. However, advanced imaging modalities such as computerized tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are highly valuable in managing patients with spinal injuries. Despite their utility, the high cost of these imaging techniques prevents them from being classified as essential. If these modalities are included as part of a national trauma care plan, their availability and functionality on a 24/7 emergency basis should be considered integral to their essential status. The American Association of Neurological Surgeons (AANS) and the Congress of Neurological Surgeons have published guidelines for the management of acute cervical spinal injuries, which address various aspects of acute spinal cord injury, including surgical management. Full compliance with these guidelines is considered desirable at specialist and tertiary care facilities. However, the cost of the infrastructure required for full compliance limits their designation as essential. Certain spinal injuries can be managed non-operatively, such as stable fractures with or without neurological injury. Some unstable bony and ligamentous injuries may also be treated either surgically or non-operatively. Non-operative management may involve adjuncts such as bed rest, cervical spine braces, halo devices, and cervical spine traction. Halo devices are particularly useful in centers with limited surgical capabilities. The ability to manage selected spinal injuries non-operatively requires training to identify appropriate cases and the necessary equipment to provide such care. These capabilities are essential in specialist and tertiary care hospitals and may also be required in general practitioner (GP)-level hospitals in rural, low-income areas. For complicated spinal cord injuries, surgical management is essential at tertiary care facilities, necessitating the presence of an orthopedic or neurological surgeon with appropriate training. In some cases, this capability may also be required at specialist-level hospitals if tertiary care facilities are not readily accessible and trained personnel are available. Burn patients are particularly vulnerable to airway and respiratory tract compromise, fluid loss, and hypovolemic shock. The ability to assess the depth and extent of burn wounds is essential at all levels of the healthcare system, as this directly impacts subsequent fluid management. Basic clean or sterile dressing materials are essential at all hospital levels, with sterile dressings being preferred where sterilization capabilities exist. Topical preparations such as silver nitrate, mafenide acetate, and silver sulfadiazine are widely used for burn wound care, with silver sulfadiazine being the most common. However, no specific preparation is endorsed by the guidelines. Debridement of necrotic tissue or external debris from burn wounds is essential at specialist and tertiary care hospitals, as is escharotomy for third-degree burns. These procedures require trained clinicians and basic surgical equipment. Skin grafting for non-healing burn wounds is also essential at these levels, requiring trained clinicians and access to a dermatome for graft harvesting. Early excision and grafting of third-degree burns have been shown to reduce mortality and improve functional outcomes, though this approach requires safeguards for hemostasis and adequate fluid and blood resuscitation capabilities. Burn wound contractures, particularly of the extremities, are a common cause of disability and are largely preventable through proper splinting and physiotherapy during wound healing. Basic expertise in splinting and physiotherapy is essential at all hospital levels, with training being the primary resource required. Even in the absence of fully trained physiotherapists, other hospital staff can be trained to provide these services. Low-cost splints can be fashioned from locally available materials if necessary. Reconstructive surgery to correct burn wound contractures or poor cosmetic outcomes from facial burns is desirable at specialist-level hospitals and essential at tertiary care facilities. This requires trained surgeons and appropriate surgical equipment. The management of wounds, both surgical and non-surgical, is critical at all levels of the healthcare system. Non-surgical management involves cleaning and dressing wounds, which is essential at all levels. Minor surgical management, such as debridement and suturing, requires expertise and basic surgical supplies, including local anesthetics, antiseptics, and sutures. Major surgical management of complicated wounds, including extensive debridement and repair of injured structures, is essential at specialist and tertiary care hospitals and may also be required at GP-level hospitals. Tetanus prophylaxis, including toxoid and antiserum, is essential at any facility with refrigeration capabilities. However, the availability of these medications cannot be deemed essential in facilities without reliable electricity or refrigeration. Rehabilitation is a critical component of injury management, particularly for fractures and burns of the extremities. Basic physiotherapy and occupational therapy are essential at all hospital levels to maximize recovery of independent function. This includes the use of splints to prevent burn wound contractures and exercises to improve range of motion and strength. While fully trained physiotherapists and occupational therapists are ideal, cost limitations may necessitate training key personnel, such as nurses or other staff, to provide these services. Prosthetic services, including the provision and fitting of prostheses, are essential at tertiary care facilities and desirable at specialist-level hospitals. Psychological counseling is also essential at all hospital levels to address the mental distress associated with severe injuries and to assist patients in adjusting to disabilities. This includes screening for psychological problems and providing appropriate treatment. Training in psychological counseling for key personnel, such as nursing and medical staff, may be necessary in the absence of fully trained mental health professionals. Specialized rehabilitative services, such as neuropsychology for cognitive dysfunction and speech pathology for communication and swallowing disorders, are desirable at specialist and tertiary care levels. Fully trained professionals in these fields are ideal but may not always be available due to cost constraints.
